fields.h1: Build a Team Quiz With a Leaderboard That Updates Live
fields.hero_description: Take the team quiz below, or build one with a live leaderboard and every answer saved to a database you own.
fields.features_heading: What Runs Behind Your Team Quiz
fields.features_subheading: Emergent builds the questions, the scoring, and the table that holds each answer from one prompt. Another prompt changes any part.
fields.feature_1:
Questions and answer keys from a prompt

Name the topic, the number of rounds, and how hard it should be. Emergent writes each question with the right answer marked and changes any question you flag before game day.
fields.feature_2:
Standings that move after each question

Team standings change after every question instead of at the end. The app shows the live leaderboard on a shared screen during a video call, and the final ranking is saved.
fields.feature_3:
Points that count for the team

Players pick a team when they open the link, and each correct answer adds a point to that team. Put bonus points for a hard round or a tiebreaker question in the same prompt.
fields.feature_4:
Every answer in a database you own

Each answer is a row in a database you own, tagged with the player, the team, and the round. Sort by question to find the one nearly every player missed, then rewrite it.
fields.feature_5:
Played on phones, with no player cap

Players answer one question per screen on a phone, at a desk or on a call. Emergent puts no cap on responses, and a company-wide all-hands runs on the same build as a team of 6.
fields.feature_6:
Your own domain and your own code

Host the quiz on your own domain, included with Emergent and paid in credits. On paid plans, export the full code to your GitHub repository and reuse it for next season.

fields.usecase_heading: How Four Workplaces Play Their Team Quiz
fields.tab_content_1:
Team Ridge beats Harbor by one answer

Every Friday at 4:00, Larch Point Analytics splits its 24 analysts into 4 teams of 6 for a 10-question team quiz on a video call. The leaderboard updates after every question. Ridge finished on 8 correct, one ahead of Harbor at 7, with Summit on 6 and Delta on 5. Each answer is saved with the round it came from.
fields.tab_content_2:
The 3 answers a new hire missed, sent to his manager

In week one, each new hire at Ardent Freight takes an 8-question quiz about how the team works. Teo Brandt scored 5 of 8. His manager, Dalia Brenner, got an email naming the 3 he missed: refund approvals, the carrier booking tool, and the on-call handover. They went through those at Friday's check-in.
fields.tab_content_3:
Zero Checkers in a studio of 14

Two weeks before its offsite, Tallow Lane Studio sends the team role quiz to its 14 designers. The results came back 5 Planner, 4 Spark, 3 Helper, 2 Closer, and 0 Checker. With no one leaning toward checking details, the studio now books a review day before every client delivery.
fields.tab_content_4:
Warehouse wins the all-hands at 9.1 correct

At the quarterly all-hands, Maren Hollow Foods runs a 12-question quiz on its own history, and 186 people answer on their phones. Scores roll up by department. The warehouse team led with an average of 9.1 correct, ahead of finance at 8.4 and sales at 7.6, and chose the charity for next quarter's food drive.

fields.howto_title: How to Run a Team Quiz
fields.howto_description: Seven steps to run a team quiz that gives every team a fair shot and ends on time, then build it with Emergent.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 Decide what the quiz is for
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Choose questions for the whole room
fields.howto_step_1_des: Settle the purpose before you write a question. Friday trivia wants quick, light rounds, while a quiz for new hires checks how the team works. A role quiz opens an offsite conversation. Put that purpose in your prompt, and Emergent drafts the quiz around it.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Mix general trivia anyone can try with questions about the company and a few about teammates, collected beforehand with their permission. Leave out anything that rewards one job title, or the same team wins every week.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Make teams of 4 to 6 people and spread each department across them, so the people who sit together are not all on one side. Name the teams before the call, and let players pick theirs when they open the link.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Hold each round to 10 questions and the whole quiz near 30 minutes. Allow 20 to 30 seconds per question on a call. Put the hardest questions in the middle round, once people have warmed up and before attention drops.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Write one tiebreaker in advance: a number question where the closest guess wins, such as the year the company opened its first office. Decide too whether the last round scores double, and put both rules in the prompt.
fields.howto_step_6_des: Play the full quiz with two colleagues who will not play on the day itself. Check every answer key, confirm the leaderboard adds points to the right team, and read each question on a phone screen before the link goes out.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Save the questions for next time
fields.howto_step_7_des: After the game, sort the answers by question. Drop the ones every team got right, rewrite the ones nobody got, and keep the rest for next quarter. A follow-up prompt adds new rounds to the same build.

faq_plan.q: What are some good team quiz ideas?
faq_plan.ref: What are some good team quiz ideas?

prov.original: What are some good team quiz ideas?

faq_plan.a: Good team quiz ideas mix rounds everyone can play: a picture round of office objects shot up close, a round matching teammates to their baby photos, a company history round, and one on the industry you work in. Finish with a number question as the tiebreaker, where the closest guess wins.

faq_plan.q: How do I create a team quiz?
faq_plan.a: Describe the occasion, the rounds, and how teams score, and Emergent's AI survey builder builds the questions and answer keys, plus the leaderboard, from that prompt. Read every question before game day, change any of them by prompting, then send players one link.

faq_plan.q: Can I make a free team quiz for my coworkers?
faq_plan.a: Yes. Emergent is free to start, and the free tier covers building and publishing. Publish the quiz and send the link to your coworkers. The team role quiz near the top of this page is also free to play, with no account and no email.

faq_plan.q: How many team quiz questions should one round have?
faq_plan.a: Ten questions make a good round: enough to separate the teams, and short enough to finish in about 5 minutes on a call. Three rounds fill a 30-minute game with time for the reveals. When the goal is to hear how people feel about working together, send a team survey instead.

faq_plan.q: How do I write team quiz questions and answers nobody argues with?
faq_plan.a: Give each question one answer you can check, and note where you checked it. Avoid questions about the best or the biggest of anything, which invite more than one fair reply. For number questions, award the closest guess. Read the answer aloud at the reveal, and the dispute ends there.

faq_plan.q: How do you keep score in a team quiz on a video call?
faq_plan.a: Let each player answer on their own phone and count every correct answer as a point for their team. The app adds the points as answers come in and shows the standings on the shared screen after each question. A disputed point can be checked against the saved answer, which sits in a database you own.

faq_plan.q: Does a team quiz help with team building at work?
faq_plan.a: It can, when teams mix people who rarely work together and the questions reward the group over one expert. Treat it as a shared half hour, not a measure of how people feel about their jobs. To measure that, run an employee engagement survey with its own questions.

faq_plan.q: What should a new hire quiz about the team ask?
faq_plan.a: Ask what a new hire needs in the first month: who approves what, which tool handles which task, and who to call after hours. Keep it to 8 questions and send each score to the manager. A missed question shows what to cover in the next one-on-one.

faq_plan.q: How do I run a team quiz for a remote team across time zones?
faq_plan.a: Pick an hour inside working time for every location and play it live, or leave the quiz open for 24 hours and rank teams on their total. The live game keeps one shared leaderboard, while the open window is fairer to distant offices. A quiz built on Emergent has no response cap, however many offices join.

faq_plan.q: Should managers see individual team quiz scores?
faq_plan.a: For a game, no: show team totals and keep each player's score out of view. For a knowledge quiz, such as one for new hires, the manager can see the score when people know that up front. Feedback about the manager belongs in a separate manager feedback survey.

results.title: Planner
results.description: Your answers lean toward mapping the work before it starts: timelines, owners, and dates. On your next project, share the plan early and leave one open slot in it for the idea that shows up late.

results.title: Spark
results.description: Your answers lean toward new ideas and fresh angles when a team gets stuck. On your next project, pair each idea with one person who can test it, and pick the one or two worth building.

results.title: Helper
results.description: Your answers lean toward keeping people connected and making sure every voice is heard. On your next project, check in with the quietest teammate first, and say so out loud when someone is overloaded.

results.title: Closer
results.description: Your answers lean toward finishing: taking a task, setting a date, and getting it done. On your next project, claim the work that is nearly done but stuck, and close it out.

results.title: Checker
results.description: Your answers lean toward the details: reading closely, testing, and catching mistakes before they ship. On your next project, ask for a review slot in the plan instead of finding time for it at the end.
